subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 12 V ideal source feeds a 3 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω resistors.
truth: The source current is 2 A.
false: The source current is 4 A.
reason: The parallel pair is 3 Ω. The source sees 3 + 3 = 6 Ω, so its current is 12/6 = 2 A.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω share an ideal 12 V source in parallel.
truth: The 4 Ω branch dissipates three times the power of the 12 Ω branch.
false: The 12 Ω branch dissipates three times the power of the 4 Ω branch.
reason: Each branch has the same voltage. Their powers are 144/4 = 36 W and 144/12 = 12 W.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: At a junction, 3 A and 5 A enter, and one outgoing branch carries 6 A. There is only one other branch.
truth: The remaining branch carries 2 A out of the junction.
false: The remaining branch carries 2 A into the junction.
reason: Current cannot accumulate at the ideal junction. Total incoming current is 8 A, so the missing outgoing current is 8 − 6 = 2 A.
formula: Sum of incoming currents = sum of outgoing currents

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal 10 V supply feeds a divider made from two 5 kΩ resistors. A 5 kΩ load is connected across the lower resistor.
truth: The loaded output voltage is 10/3 V.
false: The loaded output voltage remains 5 V.
reason: The lower resistor and load form 2.5 kΩ. The divider becomes 5 kΩ in series with 2.5 kΩ, giving 10×2.5/7.5 V.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: Two identical lamps rated for 12 V are first connected in series across an ideal 12 V supply. One lamp is then shorted. Assume each lamp has constant resistance.
truth: The power in the remaining lamp becomes four times its earlier power.
false: The power in the remaining lamp becomes twice its earlier power.
reason: Its voltage rises from 6 V to 12 V. At constant resistance, doubling voltage multiplies power by four.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A uniform wire is stretched to twice its original length while its volume and resistivity remain unchanged.
truth: Its resistance becomes four times the original resistance.
false: Its resistance becomes twice the original resistance.
reason: Constant volume means that doubling length halves area. R = ρL/A therefore grows by a factor of 2/(1/2).

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: Two wires have the same material and length. The diameter of wire X is twice the diameter of wire Y.
truth: Wire X has one quarter of the resistance of wire Y.
false: Wire X has half the resistance of wire Y.
reason: Cross-sectional area is proportional to diameter squared. X has four times the area, so one quarter of the resistance.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 500 W heater runs for 20 minutes and a 100 W fan runs for 2 hours.
truth: Their total energy use is 11/30 kWh.
false: Their total energy use is 0.7 kWh.
reason: The heater uses 0.5×(1/3) kWh and the fan uses 0.1×2 kWh. Add the energies, not the operating times.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A device is specified as 24 V, 48 W. It is treated as a constant resistor and connected to 12 V.
truth: It consumes 12 W.
false: It consumes 24 W.
reason: Its resistance is 24²/48 = 12 Ω. At 12 V, power is 12²/12 = 12 W.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A battery transfers 180 C through a load in 30 seconds while maintaining 12 V.
truth: The load receives 2160 J.
false: The load receives 360 J.
reason: Voltage is energy transferred per coulomb. Multiply the 12 J/C by 180 C.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery before a dielectric is inserted fully between its plates. Capacitance doubles and no charge leaks away.
truth: The stored energy becomes half its initial value.
false: The stored energy doubles.
reason: An isolated capacitor keeps its charge. Since energy is Q²/(2C), doubling capacitance halves the energy.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: Two initially uncharged capacitors, 2 μF and 4 μF, are connected in series across 12 V.
truth: The 2 μF capacitor has 8 V across it.
false: The 2 μF capacitor has 4 V across it.
reason: Series capacitors carry equal charge. Voltages divide inversely with capacitance; the smaller capacitor gets twice the voltage.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 2 μF capacitor charged to 10 V is connected in parallel, with matching polarity, to an uncharged 3 μF capacitor. Ignore leakage and external sources.
truth: Their final common voltage is 4 V.
false: Their final common voltage is 5 V.
reason: Total charge is 20 μC and combined capacitance is 5 μF. Charge conservation gives 20/5 = 4 V.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An initially uncharged capacitor is charged through a resistor from a DC step. At one time constant the voltage is about 63.2% of its final value.
truth: The resistor voltage at that instant is about 36.8% of the supply.
false: The resistor voltage at that instant is about 63.2% of the supply.
reason: The capacitor and resistor voltages sum to the supply, so the resistor has the remaining 100 − 63.2 percent.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A capacitor discharges through a fixed resistor. At time t its voltage has fallen to half its starting value.
truth: Its stored energy has fallen to one quarter of its starting value.
false: Its stored energy has fallen to half its starting value.
reason: Stored energy depends on voltage squared, so a voltage factor of 1/2 gives an energy factor of 1/4.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 0.5 H ideal inductor carries 4 A. Its current then falls to 2 A.
truth: The energy released is 3 J.
false: The energy released is 1 J.
reason: The initial energy is 4 J and final energy is 1 J. The difference is 3 J.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal inductor has been connected in series with a resistor to a DC source for a very long time.
truth: Its voltage is zero while a nonzero steady current can flow.
false: Its current must be zero because its voltage is zero.
reason: For an ideal inductor, voltage depends on the rate of change of current. Steady current has zero rate of change.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A series circuit has resistance 6 Ω and net inductive reactance 8 Ω. It is supplied with 100 V RMS.
truth: Its real power is 600 W.
false: Its real power is 1000 W.
reason: Impedance magnitude is 10 Ω, so current is 10 A. Only resistance consumes real power: 10²×6 = 600 W.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A sine-wave voltage has 100 V RMS and is applied to a purely resistive 50 Ω load.
truth: Its average power is 200 W.
false: Its average power is 400 W.
reason: RMS values give the heating effect directly. No extra factor of two is needed.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal capacitor remains connected to a sinusoidal source of fixed RMS voltage. The source frequency doubles.
truth: Its RMS current doubles.
false: Its RMS current halves.
reason: Capacitive reactance falls by half when frequency doubles. With voltage unchanged, the current doubles.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A series RLC circuit is exactly at resonance and has a nonzero resistance.
truth: Supply voltage and current are in phase.
false: Supply current leads the voltage by 90°.
reason: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel; total impedance is purely resistive.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal transformer has 600 primary turns and 150 secondary turns. A 240 V primary supply feeds a 30 Ω secondary load.
truth: The primary current is 0.5 A.
false: The primary current is 2 A.
reason: Secondary voltage is 60 V and secondary current is 2 A. Output power is 120 W, so input current is 120/240 A.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal transformer has a secondary-to-primary turns ratio of 2. A 100 Ω resistor is connected across the secondary.
truth: The resistance seen from the primary is 25 Ω.
false: The resistance seen from the primary is 200 Ω.
reason: Reflected resistance is scaled by the square of the primary-to-secondary turns ratio, which is (1/2)².

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A transformer delivers 800 W while drawing 1000 W at the same operating point.
truth: Its losses are 200 W and its efficiency is 80%.
false: Its losses are 250 W and its efficiency is 80%.
reason: Loss is input minus output, while efficiency is output divided by input. These use different operations.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A conventional transformer designed for sinusoidal AC is connected directly to a steady DC supply.
truth: It cannot provide continuous transformer action from a steady flux.
false: It supplies continuous secondary voltage because its turns ratio is unchanged.
reason: Faraday's law requires changing flux. After the switching transient, steady flux cannot induce continuous secondary EMF. Primary overheating is also a risk.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A coil is rotated so that its normal changes from parallel to a uniform magnetic field to perpendicular to that field.
truth: Its magnetic flux changes from maximum magnitude to zero.
false: Its magnetic flux changes from zero to maximum magnitude.
reason: Flux is BA cos θ where θ is measured between the field and the coil normal.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 100-turn coil experiences a uniform flux decrease from 0.03 Wb to 0.01 Wb per turn in 0.1 s.
truth: The magnitude of the average induced EMF is 20 V.
false: The magnitude of the average induced EMF is 2 V.
reason: Each turn loses 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s. Multiply the rate of change by all 100 turns.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field exactly along the field direction.
truth: The magnetic force on it is zero.
false: The magnetic force is maximum.
reason: The velocity and field are parallel, so sin θ = 0 in the magnetic-force expression.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A machine lifts a 20 kg mass vertically by 3 m in 5 s. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore losses.
truth: Its useful average power is 120 W.
false: Its useful average power is 600 W.
reason: The useful work is 600 J. Power divides that work by the 5 s interval.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: Equal masses of the same substance at 20°C and 80°C are mixed in an insulated container, with no phase change and constant heat capacity.
truth: The final temperature is 50°C.
false: The final temperature is 60°C.
reason: Equal heat capacities mean the hotter mass loses exactly the heat gained by the colder mass; the final temperature is their mean.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A Celsius thermometer rises from 10°C to 30°C.
truth: The temperature rise is 20 K.
false: The temperature rise is 293.15 K.
reason: Celsius and kelvin increments have equal size. The offset applies to absolute readings, not differences.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal full-wave rectifier is supplied by a 50 Hz sine wave.
truth: Its unfiltered output has a repetition frequency of 100 Hz.
false: Its unfiltered output has a repetition frequency of 25 Hz.
reason: Both input half-cycles produce output pulses with the same polarity, so there are two pulses per input cycle.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 5 V ideal Zener regulator uses a 1 kΩ series resistor from 12 V. A load draws 3 mA, and the Zener is in breakdown.
truth: The Zener current is 4 mA.
false: The Zener current is 7 mA.
reason: The series resistor carries (12−5)/1000 = 7 mA. The load takes 3 mA, leaving 4 mA through the Zener.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An LED has a forward drop of 2 V and is to carry 10 mA from a 5 V DC supply.
truth: A 300 Ω series resistor gives the intended current under these assumptions.
false: A 500 Ω series resistor gives the intended current under these assumptions.
reason: The resistor must drop only 5−2 = 3 V, not the entire supply voltage.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A transistor is in active mode with base current 20 μA and collector current 2 mA.
truth: Its DC current gain is 100.
false: Its DC current gain is 0.01.
reason: Convert to the same units: 2 mA is 2000 μA. Divide collector current by base current.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A BJT switch is already in saturation and the collector load and supply remain fixed.
truth: Increasing base drive need not produce the active-region proportional increase in collector current.
false: Collector current must keep rising exactly as β times base current.
reason: In saturation, the external collector circuit largely limits the current. The active-region gain equation no longer predicts an unrestricted increase.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A reverse-biased photodiode is used to detect a changing light level within its normal operating range.
truth: Incident light can change its reverse photocurrent.
false: It must emit light to measure the incident light.
reason: A photodiode converts incoming optical energy into a measurable electrical response. Light emission describes an LED's intended function.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ammeter has resistance 1 Ω and is mistakenly placed directly across an ideal 12 V source.
truth: The meter branch attempts to draw 12 A.
false: The meter branch draws zero current because ammeters only measure.
reason: Its small internal resistance becomes the entire load across the source. An ammeter belongs in series with the load.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 10 kΩ voltmeter is connected across one 10 kΩ resistor in an equal-resistor divider driven by 12 V.
truth: The reading is 4 V.
false: The reading is 6 V.
reason: The meter parallels the lower resistor, reducing it to 5 kΩ. The divider output is 12×5/(10+5) = 4 V.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A movement reaches full scale at 1 mA and has resistance 100 Ω. It is to measure 10 V at full scale.
truth: The additional series resistance is 9900 Ω.
false: The additional series resistance is 10000 Ω.
reason: Total required resistance is 10/0.001 = 10000 Ω. Subtract the movement's existing 100 Ω.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A 100 Ω movement carries 1 mA at full scale and is shunted to measure 101 mA total.
truth: A 1 Ω shunt is required.
false: A 100 Ω shunt is required.
reason: The shunt carries 100 mA while the movement carries 1 mA. Both branches have 0.1 V across them.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: One full sine-wave cycle spans 5 horizontal divisions at 2 ms per division.
truth: The frequency is 100 Hz.
false: The frequency is 10 Hz.
reason: The period is 10 ms = 0.01 s, whose reciprocal is 100 Hz.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A waveform spans 6 vertical divisions peak to peak at 2 V per division. It is symmetric about zero.
truth: Its positive peak is 6 V.
false: Its positive peak is 12 V.
reason: Peak-to-peak voltage is 12 V. Symmetry about zero makes either peak magnitude half this value.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A meter reads 49 V when a reference value is 50 V.
truth: The signed relative error is −2%.
false: The signed relative error is +2%.
reason: Signed error is measured minus reference. Here it is −1 V, divided by the 50 V reference.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: Repeated measurements are tightly clustered at 9.0 V, while a reliable reference is 10.0 V.
truth: The readings are precise but show a systematic accuracy problem.
false: The readings must be accurate because their spread is small.
reason: Precision concerns repeatability. Accuracy concerns closeness to the reference; a consistent offset can preserve precision but spoil accuracy.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A strain gauge is bonded to a beam and its resistance changes as the beam stretches.
truth: It can convert mechanical strain into an electrical resistance change.
false: It directly converts strain into a fixed-frequency radio signal without supporting circuitry.
reason: The gauge's primary output is a resistance change. Further circuits are needed to measure or transmit it.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A conventional AM signal has a 1 MHz carrier and a single 2 kHz modulation tone.
truth: Its sidebands occur at 998 kHz and 1002 kHz.
false: Its sidebands occur at 2 kHz and 2000 kHz.
reason: AM sidebands are at the carrier minus and plus the message frequency.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A conventional AM envelope has maximum amplitude 9 V and minimum amplitude 3 V.
truth: Its modulation index is 0.5.
false: Its modulation index is 2.
reason: Use the difference divided by the sum of envelope extremes, not the reverse ratio.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A baseband signal contains frequencies only up to 4 kHz and is ideally sampled at 10 ksample/s.
truth: The rate exceeds twice the highest signal frequency.
false: The rate is below the Nyquist minimum.
reason: Twice 4 kHz is 8 kHz. The stated 10 ksample/s rate exceeds that threshold under ideal band-limited assumptions.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal uniform ADC has 8 output bits, and another has 10 bits over the same input range.
truth: The second ADC has four times as many code levels.
false: The second ADC has twice as many code levels.
reason: The number of levels is 2 to the power of bit count. Adding two bits multiplies levels by four.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: Two equal-frequency waves of equal amplitude arrive exactly 180° out of phase.
truth: Their ideal resultant amplitude is zero.
false: Their ideal resultant amplitude is twice either amplitude.
reason: Equal and opposite instantaneous displacements cancel. Reinforcement requires equal phase rather than opposite phase.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A two-input NAND gate receives inputs A = 1 and B = 1, and its output is passed through an inverter.
truth: The final output is 1.
false: The final output is 0.
reason: The NAND output is 0 for inputs 1,1. The following inverter changes 0 to 1.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An alarm should activate if exactly one of two sensors is high, but remain off if both are high.
truth: An XOR function matches this requirement.
false: An OR function matches this requirement.
reason: XOR is high only for unequal binary inputs. OR is also high when both inputs are high, so it does not meet the requirement.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A binary counter has three flip-flops and uses all possible states before repeating.
truth: It can count through eight distinct states.
false: It can count through six distinct states.
reason: Three binary storage elements represent 2³ combinations, counting 000 through 111.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A metal-cased appliance has protective earthing, and its live wire touches the case.
truth: A suitable low-resistance earth path can help a protective device disconnect the supply.
false: The earth connection intentionally keeps the metal case at live voltage.
reason: Protective earthing limits touch voltage and provides a fault-current path that enables appropriate protection. It is not a normal supply connection to the case.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A fuse is rated for current and is installed in series in the live conductor of a circuit.
truth: Opening the fuse interrupts the live supply path to the load.
false: Opening the fuse connects the load directly to earth.
reason: A fuse operates by breaking its series path during excessive current. It does not create an earth connection.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: An ideal diode is reverse biased and remains below breakdown.
truth: The ideal model predicts zero current through it.
false: The ideal model predicts zero voltage across it and unlimited current.
reason: The ideal reverse-biased diode is an open circuit. A short-circuit model belongs to a forward-conducting ideal diode.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A pure silicon crystal is doped with a small amount of a pentavalent donor impurity.
truth: Electrons become the majority mobile carriers.
false: Holes become the majority mobile carriers.
reason: A donor contributes an extra electron to form n-type material. Acceptor doping instead produces p-type material.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A solenoid's current direction is reversed while its geometry remains the same.
truth: Its north and south magnetic poles interchange.
false: Its magnetic poles stay unchanged because the winding shape is unchanged.
reason: The magnetic-field direction follows the current direction through the winding. Reversing current reverses the field.

subject: Science & Engineering
scenario: A constant 2 A current flows for 3 minutes through a conductor.
truth: The charge passing a cross-section is 360 C.
false: The charge passing a cross-section is 6 C.
reason: Convert minutes to seconds before multiplying by current: 2×180 = 360.

subject: Computers
scenario: A four-bit unsigned register contains 1111₂. The instruction adds 1 and keeps only the lowest four bits.
truth: The stored result is 0000₂.
false: The stored result is 10000₂.
reason: The exact sum needs five bits. Keeping only four drops the carry and stores zero.

subject: Computers
scenario: The eight-bit pattern 11111111₂ is interpreted once as unsigned and once as two's complement.
truth: The two interpretations give 255 and −1 respectively.
false: Both interpretations give 255.
reason: The pattern's meaning depends on the number representation. An all-ones two's-complement pattern represents −1.

subject: Computers
scenario: The hexadecimal value 2A is converted to decimal, then increased by decimal 6.
truth: The final decimal value is 48.
false: The final decimal value is 42.
reason: 2A₁₆ is 2×16+10 = 42. The requested addition occurs after conversion.
formula: Positional value = sum of digit × base^position

subject: Computers
scenario: An eight-bit two's-complement adder adds 01111111₂ and 00000001₂.
truth: The stored pattern represents −128 and signed overflow has occurred.
false: The stored pattern represents +128 without overflow.
reason: The mathematical answer 128 is outside the signed eight-bit range −128 to 127. The stored 10000000 pattern is −128.

subject: Computers
scenario: A 16-bit integer 0x1234 is stored at consecutive byte addresses 100 and 101 using little-endian order.
truth: Address 100 contains 0x34.
false: Address 100 contains 0x12.
reason: Little-endian order puts the least significant byte at the lowest address. This concerns byte order, not the value of the integer.

subject: Computers
scenario: A byte-addressable memory has 12 address lines and no bank switching.
truth: It has 4096 separately addressable bytes.
false: It has 4096 separately addressable bits.
reason: Twelve address bits identify 2¹² addresses. Each address holds one byte by the stated design.

subject: Computers
scenario: A memory device has 1024 locations and each location holds 16 bits.
truth: Its total capacity is 2048 bytes.
false: Its total capacity is 1024 bytes.
reason: Capacity is locations times bits per location; divide bits by eight to get bytes.

subject: Computers
scenario: A cache hit takes 2 ns and occurs 90% of the time. A miss has a total access time of 22 ns, including the lookup.
truth: The average access time is 4 ns.
false: The average access time is 24 ns.
reason: Weight the total hit and miss times by their probabilities. Do not add the miss time to every access.
formula: Average = hit fraction × hit time + miss fraction × total miss time

subject: Computers
scenario: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines. Memory blocks map by block number modulo 4. Blocks 1 and 5 are accessed alternately.
truth: Both blocks compete for the same cache line.
false: The blocks necessarily occupy two different cache lines.
reason: Both block numbers leave remainder 1 on division by 4. They therefore map to line 1.

subject: Computers
scenario: A 1 KiB file is stored on a file system allocating whole 4 KiB clusters, without compression or inline storage.
truth: Its data allocation is 4 KiB.
false: Its data allocation must be exactly 1 KiB.
reason: A partly used cluster is still allocated as a whole. This does not mean the logical file length changes.

subject: Computers
scenario: A machine loses electrical power after data has been written successfully to an SSD but before an unsaved edit leaves RAM.
truth: The SSD data normally persists, while the RAM-only edit is lost.
false: The unsaved RAM-only edit is guaranteed to persist while the SSD data is lost.
reason: SSD storage is nonvolatile; ordinary working RAM is volatile. Successful persistent writes differ from unsaved working changes.

subject: Computers
scenario: Process P waits for a disk read while process Q is ready to run on a single CPU.
truth: The operating system can run Q while P is blocked.
false: The CPU must stay idle until P's disk read completes.
reason: Scheduling another ready process can overlap CPU work with an outstanding I/O operation. A blocked process does not need the CPU while waiting.

subject: Computers
scenario: Two running processes each hold one resource and wait indefinitely for a resource held by the other, with no forced release.
truth: This describes a circular-wait deadlock situation.
false: This proves both processes are making progress concurrently.
reason: Each process prevents the other from obtaining what it needs. With the stated indefinite wait and no release mechanism, neither progresses.

subject: Computers
scenario: A user renames a file from report.txt to report.jpg without converting its contents.
truth: The name change alone does not convert the text into JPEG image data.
false: The file contents become a valid JPEG solely because the suffix changes.
reason: An extension is part of a name. Actual format depends on the stored bytes and their structure.

subject: Computers
scenario: In a Unix-style permission model, a regular file has mode 640.
truth: The owner may read and write, the group may read, and others have no permission.
false: The owner may execute the file because the first digit is 6.
reason: Permission weights are read=4, write=2 and execute=1. Six is 4+2 and contains no execute bit.

subject: Computers
scenario: The processor has just fetched an instruction and advances its program counter in a simple sequential instruction model.
truth: The program counter identifies where the next instruction is to be fetched.
false: The program counter must contain the arithmetic result of the current instruction.
reason: The program counter tracks instruction sequencing. Arithmetic results are usually stored in other registers or memory.

subject: Computers
scenario: A processor's clock frequency rises, but the program now needs twice as many cycles per instruction and the instruction count is unchanged. Clock frequency rises by only 25%.
truth: The execution time becomes 1.6 times the original.
false: The execution time falls to 0.8 times the original.
reason: Execution time is instruction count times cycles per instruction divided by clock frequency. The ratio is 2/1.25.
formula: Time = instruction count × CPI / clock rate

subject: Computers
scenario: A program spends half its time in a section that is made twice as fast; the other half is unchanged.
truth: Overall execution time falls to 75% of its original value.
false: Overall execution time falls to 50% of its original value.
reason: The improved half now takes a quarter of the original total time. Add the unchanged half.
formula: New time ratio = unchanged fraction + improved fraction/speedup

subject: Computers
scenario: A computer sends a scanned document to a printer after receiving it from a scanner.
truth: The scanner is the input device and the printer is the output device in this operation.
false: The printer is the input device because it receives data from the computer.
reason: Device classification is relative to the computer: information enters through the scanner and leaves through the printer.

subject: Computers
scenario: Two computers in the same IPv4 subnet exchange Ethernet frames through a switch with a learned MAC table.
truth: The switch can forward using the destination MAC address.
false: The switch must use the email address of the recipient to select a port.
reason: Ordinary Ethernet switching uses link-layer addresses. Email addresses are application-level identifiers.

subject: Computers
scenario: A host has IPv4 address 192.168.4.70 with subnet mask 255.255.255.192.
truth: Its /26 subnet starts at 192.168.4.64.
false: Its /26 subnet starts at 192.168.4.0.
reason: The last-octet block size is 64. Address 70 belongs to the block 64 through 127.

subject: Computers
scenario: An IPv4 /27 subnet uses the conventional network and broadcast reservations.
truth: It supports 30 ordinary host addresses.
false: It supports 32 ordinary host addresses.
reason: There are five host bits, giving 32 total addresses. Two are conventionally reserved.

subject: Computers
scenario: A website opens when its numeric IP address is used, but its name fails to resolve. Connectivity otherwise works.
truth: Investigating DNS configuration is a reasonable first step.
false: Replacing the display monitor is the most direct explanation for the symptom.
reason: DNS maps names to addresses. Working address-based connectivity with failed name resolution points toward that mapping stage.

subject: Computers
scenario: A browser receives a valid HTTP 404 response from a server.
truth: A server answered, but the requested resource was not found.
false: The response proves that no network communication with a server occurred.
reason: An HTTP status response itself requires an HTTP exchange. A 404 concerns the requested resource, not the absence of any connection.

subject: Computers
scenario: A message must be delivered reliably and in order over a transport connection, even if packets are retransmitted.
truth: TCP provides mechanisms supporting those requirements.
false: UDP by itself guarantees both ordered delivery and retransmission.
reason: TCP tracks sequence and acknowledgements. UDP does not itself supply those reliability guarantees.

subject: Computers
scenario: A 1200-byte payload is sent with 300 bytes of overhead over a 12000 bit/s link.
truth: The transmission time for the complete frame is 1 second.
false: The transmission time for the complete frame is 0.8 second.
reason: The link sends payload and overhead: 1500 bytes = 12000 bits. At 12000 bit/s, this takes one second.
formula: Time = (payload bytes + overhead bytes) × 8 / bit rate

subject: Computers
scenario: A data link operates full duplex at 10 Mbit/s in each direction.
truth: It can carry traffic in both directions simultaneously.
false: It must alternate directions because full duplex permits only one transmitter at a time.
reason: Full duplex provides simultaneous two-way communication. Alternating directions describes half duplex.

subject: Computers
scenario: A user can send email from a mail client but needs a protocol to synchronize received messages and folders with a server.
truth: IMAP is suited to the synchronization task.
false: SMTP alone supplies the mailbox-folder synchronization function.
reason: SMTP is used for sending/relaying mail. IMAP is designed for accessing and synchronizing server mailboxes.

subject: Computers
scenario: A login requires a memorized password and a time-based code from a separately possessed authenticator.
truth: The two requirements can represent knowledge and possession factors.
false: Both requirements are knowledge factors simply because both are typed.
reason: The factor category depends on what proves identity, not on whether the user types characters. A separately held authenticator is a possession factor.

subject: Computers
scenario: An email urges a user to enter a banking password on an unfamiliar look-alike domain.
truth: The user should verify through a known official channel instead of trusting the link.
false: The urgent wording makes the unfamiliar domain trustworthy.
reason: Impersonation and pressure are common phishing tactics. Independent verification avoids relying on the potentially deceptive message.

subject: Computers
scenario: A message is encrypted with a recipient's public key in a suitable public-key encryption system.
truth: The corresponding private key is needed to decrypt it.
false: Any person holding the public key can necessarily decrypt it.
reason: The public key may be shared for encryption, while the matching private key is kept secret for decryption.

subject: Computers
scenario: A downloaded file is checked against a trusted published cryptographic hash.
truth: A matching hash can support an integrity check.
false: A matching hash by itself proves the file is harmless software.
reason: A hash comparison checks whether bytes match the trusted reference. Harmfulness is a different property and requires additional assessment.

subject: Computers
scenario: A backup disk is permanently writable from a computer that becomes infected with ransomware.
truth: The writable backup may also be at risk.
false: The backup is guaranteed safe merely because it is on a second disk.
reason: A second disk is not the same as isolation. Malware with write access can alter reachable backup data.

subject: Computers
scenario: An Orders table stores CustomerID values that reference a Customers table's primary key.
truth: A foreign-key constraint can reject an order referring to a nonexistent customer.
false: A foreign-key constraint automatically encrypts the customer's data.
reason: Referential integrity concerns valid relationships between rows. Encryption is a separate security feature.

subject: Computers
scenario: Customer phone numbers are copied into every order row, and the same customer's number changes.
truth: Storing customer details separately can reduce inconsistent duplicate updates.
false: Repeating the number in every order guarantees that all copies update together.
reason: Repeated attributes create an update anomaly unless managed explicitly. Separating entities helps keep one authoritative customer record.

subject: Computers
scenario: A table has three rows with a Score column containing 10, NULL and 20. Standard SQL COUNT(Score) is evaluated.
truth: The result is 2.
false: The result is 3.
reason: COUNT(column) ignores NULL values; COUNT(*) counts rows. Two scores are non-NULL.

subject: Computers
scenario: Rows are grouped by Department, and only groups with AVG(Salary) above a threshold should remain.
truth: A HAVING condition can filter the aggregate groups.
false: A plain WHERE AVG(Salary) condition is the standard way to filter groups at that stage.
reason: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the resulting groups using aggregates.

subject: Computers
scenario: A database transaction transfers funds by debiting one account and crediting another.
truth: Atomicity aims to make the transfer's changes happen together or not at all.
false: Atomicity requires the debit to be permanently committed before the credit is attempted.
reason: An all-or-nothing transaction prevents a partial transfer from leaving only one side applied.

subject: Computers
scenario: Cell C2 contains =$A2*B$1 and the formula is copied one column right and one row down to D3.
truth: The copied formula is =$A3*C$1.
false: The copied formula is =$B3*C$2.
reason: The dollar sign fixes column A and row 1. Unfixed row 2 shifts to 3 and column B shifts to C.

subject: Computers
scenario: A spreadsheet computes SUM(A1:A3), where A1=2, A2=3 and A3=5. A4 contains 100.
truth: The result is 10.
false: The result is 110.
reason: The specified range stops at A3, so A4 is excluded.
formula: SUM adds only the referenced cells

subject: Computers
scenario: A long report uses heading styles consistently before inserting an automatic table of contents.
truth: The styles help the program identify entries for the table of contents.
false: Manually making every heading bold necessarily provides the same structural information.
reason: Styles assign document structure. Bold formatting alone does not identify heading levels to the table-of-contents mechanism.

subject: Computers
scenario: A sorted list is searched by repeatedly halving the remaining search interval.
truth: Binary search is appropriate for this stated organization.
false: The halving strategy is guaranteed to work on any unsorted list without preparation.
reason: Binary search relies on ordering to decide which half cannot contain the target. Unsorted data removes that guarantee.

subject: Computers
scenario: A loop starts with s=0 and adds i for each integer i from 1 through 4 inclusive.
truth: The final s is 10.
false: The final s is 6.
reason: The inclusive endpoint contributes 4, so add 1+2+3+4.

subject: Computers
scenario: A stack receives Push(A), Push(B), Pop(), then Push(C), followed by Pop().
truth: The final Pop returns C.
false: The final Pop returns A.
reason: The first Pop removes B. Pushing C places it above A, so C is removed next under last-in-first-out order.

subject: Computers
scenario: A queue receives Enqueue(A), Enqueue(B), Dequeue(), Enqueue(C), then Dequeue().
truth: The final Dequeue returns B.
false: The final Dequeue returns C.
reason: The first removal takes A. The remaining order is B then C, so the next removal takes B under first-in-first-out order.

subject: Computers
scenario: A permission rule is NOT(A OR B).
truth: Access under this rule requires both A and B to be false.
false: Access under this rule requires at least one of A and B to be false.
reason: By De Morgan's law, NOT(A OR B) equals (NOT A) AND (NOT B). Both conditions must be false.

subject: Computers
scenario: A received word fails its required even-parity check.
truth: At least one bit error is detected under the parity model.
false: The parity failure tells the receiver exactly which bit to correct.
reason: Parity detects inconsistency but a single parity bit does not identify the error position.

subject: Computers
scenario: Two bits flip in a word protected only by a single even-parity bit.
truth: The parity check can miss this error.
false: A single even-parity check must detect every two-bit error.
reason: An even number of flips preserves parity. This is a known limitation of a single parity bit.

subject: Computers
scenario: A desktop works with an external display while its built-in display remains blank.
truth: The symptom can be consistent with a display-path fault rather than a total CPU failure.
false: The symptom proves that every CPU operation has stopped.
reason: Producing working external video requires substantial system operation. The evidence narrows the investigation but does not identify one exact faulty component.

subject: Computers
scenario: A compiler rejects a program because a required closing bracket is missing.
truth: This is a syntax problem caught before a normal run of that program.
false: This proves the program's numerical algorithm is incorrect on every input.
reason: Syntax determines whether code is well formed. An algorithmic correctness claim is different and cannot be established from this bracket error alone.

subject: Computers
scenario: Firmware is stored in nonvolatile flash memory and supports updates.
truth: The stored instructions can persist without power and can still be rewritten by an update procedure.
false: Nonvolatile storage means the instructions can never be rewritten.
reason: Nonvolatile describes retention without power. Reprogrammability is a separate property; flash supports controlled rewriting.

subject: Computers
scenario: An unsigned 10-bit sensor value must fit in an unsigned 8-bit field without loss for every possible input.
truth: The smaller field cannot represent every possible sensor value.
false: The smaller field can represent all values because both are unsigned.
reason: Ten bits support 1024 values, but eight bits support only 256. At least some values cannot be represented losslessly.

subject: Computers
scenario: A router links two different IP networks, while a basic Ethernet switch connects devices inside one LAN.
truth: The router makes network-layer forwarding decisions between the networks.
false: The basic switch must route all traffic between unrelated IP networks by default.
reason: Routing selects paths using network-layer information. Ordinary layer-2 switching uses MAC addresses within its switching domain.

subject: Computers
scenario: A shortcut points to a document. The shortcut itself is deleted, while the target file remains unchanged.
truth: The document may still be opened directly at its actual location.
false: Deleting the shortcut necessarily erases the target document's contents.
reason: A shortcut is a reference to a target; it is not generally the target file itself.

subject: Computers
scenario: A transfer rate is 8 Mbit/s and decimal SI units are used, with all overhead ignored.
truth: The rate is 1 megabyte per second.
false: The rate is 8 megabytes per second.
reason: One byte has eight bits, so divide the bit rate by eight.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20% of the increased price.
truth: The final price is 4% below the starting price.
false: The final price equals the starting price.
reason: The multipliers act on different bases. Their product is 1.2×0.8 = 0.96.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A worker's wage increases by 25%. Prices of everything the worker buys also increase by 25%, with the spending pattern unchanged.
truth: The wage buys the same quantity as before.
false: The wage buys 25% more than before.
reason: Real purchasing quantity depends on the wage-to-price ratio. Both numerator and denominator have the same multiplier.
formula: Real ratio = wage multiplier / price multiplier

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A trader marks an item 50% above cost and offers a 20% discount on that marked price.
truth: The sale yields a 20% profit on cost.
false: The sale yields a 30% profit on cost.
reason: The selling-price multiplier is 1.5×0.8 = 1.2. Percentage markup and discount cannot simply be subtracted.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Two articles are sold at ₹120 each. One sale gives a 20% gain and the other a 20% loss, both measured on cost.
truth: There is an overall loss of ₹10.
false: There is no overall gain or loss.
reason: The costs are 120/1.2 = 100 and 120/0.8 = 150. Total cost 250 exceeds total selling price 240.
formula: CP = SP/(1+gain rate) or SP/(1−loss rate)

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3:2. Ten litres of water are added and the ratio becomes 1:1.
truth: The original mixture had 50 litres.
false: The original mixture had 25 litres.
reason: Write original amounts as 3k and 2k. Equality after adding water gives 3k = 2k+10, so k=10 and total=5k.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A 20-litre solution is 30% salt by volume under an ideal additive-volume model. Five litres of pure water are added.
truth: The new concentration is 24%.
false: The new concentration is 25%.
reason: Salt stays at 6 litres while total volume becomes 25 litres. Concentration is 6/25.
formula: New concentration = unchanged solute / new volume

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A container holds 10 litres of pure milk. Two litres are removed and replaced with water; the same operation is then repeated after complete mixing.
truth: The final amount of milk is 6.4 litres.
false: The final amount of milk is 6 litres.
reason: Each replacement retains 8/10 of the milk present before that operation. The second removal includes some water.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: The mean of five numbers is 12. One number, 8, is replaced by 18.
truth: The new mean is 14.
false: The new mean is 22.
reason: The total increases by 10 across five entries, so the mean increases by 2.
formula: New mean = old mean + change in total/count

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A class of 20 students has mean score 60, and another class of 30 has mean score 80.
truth: The combined mean is 72.
false: The combined mean is 70.
reason: Use the group sizes as weights, rather than averaging the two means equally.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Every observation in a dataset is increased by 7.
truth: Its mean rises by 7, but its standard deviation stays the same.
false: Both its mean and standard deviation rise by 7.
reason: Adding a constant shifts the centre without changing any deviation from the mean.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Every observation in a dataset is multiplied by 3.
truth: Its variance becomes nine times the original variance.
false: Its variance becomes three times the original variance.
reason: Deviations multiply by 3 and squared deviations therefore multiply by 9.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation: grouped/ungrouped data
scenario: The dataset is 2, 4, 6 and population variance is requested.
truth: The population variance is 8/3.
false: The population variance is 4.
reason: The mean is 4; squared deviations are 4,0,4. Population variance divides their sum by 3, not by 2.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A fair coin is tossed twice. It is known that at least one toss is heads.
truth: The probability that both tosses are heads is 1/3.
false: The probability that both tosses are heads is 1/2.
reason: The condition leaves HH, HT and TH as three equally likely outcomes. Only HH meets the target condition.
formula: Conditional probability = favourable retained outcomes / all retained outcomes

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement.
truth: The probability that both are blue is 1/10.
false: The probability that both are blue is 4/25.
reason: After a blue ball is drawn, only one blue remains among four balls. The draws are not independent.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Probability: occurrence, exhaustive and mutually exclusive events
scenario: Two events A and B are mutually exclusive, with probabilities 0.3 and 0.4.
truth: The probability of A or B is 0.7.
false: The probability of A and B is 0.12.
reason: Mutually exclusive events have zero intersection. Their union probability is the sum, but multiplication would assume a different relationship.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Universal sets, Venn diagrams, union, intersection, difference and complements
scenario: Of 50 students, 28 study physics, 25 study chemistry and 10 study both.
truth: Seven students study neither subject.
false: Seventeen students study neither subject.
reason: The union is 28+25−10 = 43. Subtract that from the class total to find those in neither set.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A completes a task in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work together for 3 days at constant independent rates.
truth: They finish 5/12 of the task in those 3 days.
false: They finish 1/5 of the task in those 3 days.
reason: Their combined daily rate is 1/12+1/18 = 5/36. Multiply by 3 days.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A can finish a task in 10 days and B in 15 days. A works alone for 2 days; then B finishes the remainder alone.
truth: B needs 12 additional days.
false: B needs 8 additional days.
reason: A completes 1/5 of the work, leaving 4/5. At 1/15 per day, B needs 12 days.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: An inlet fills a tank in 6 hours and an outlet empties a full tank in 9 hours. Both are opened in an initially empty tank, with constant rates.
truth: The tank fills in 18 hours.
false: The tank fills in 3 hours.
reason: The rates oppose each other. Net filling rate is 1/6−1/9 = 1/18 tank per hour.
formula: Net rate = inlet rate − outlet rate

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A vehicle travels equal distances at 30 km/h and 60 km/h, with no stops.
truth: The average speed is 40 km/h.
false: The average speed is 45 km/h.
reason: Equal distances at different speeds take different times; total distance divided by total time gives the harmonic mean.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Two trains of lengths 100 m and 150 m move in opposite directions at 36 km/h and 54 km/h.
truth: They take 10 seconds to pass each other completely.
false: They take 50 seconds to pass each other completely.
reason: Combined length is 250 m. Opposite directions give relative speed 90 km/h = 25 m/s.
formula: Time = sum of lengths / relative speed

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A 120 m train moving at 20 m/s overtakes a runner moving in the same direction at 5 m/s.
truth: It takes 8 seconds to pass the runner completely.
false: It takes 4.8 seconds to pass the runner completely.
reason: Same-direction relative speed is 20−5 = 15 m/s. The relative distance is the train's length.
formula: Time = train length / difference in speeds

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Two equal principals earn simple interest for the same time, one at 6% and the other at 9% per year.
truth: The interest amounts are in the ratio 2:3.
false: The final amounts are necessarily in the ratio 2:3.
reason: With equal principal and time, interest scales with rate. Final amounts also include principal and do not have that ratio in general.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: An amount of ₹1200 becomes ₹1440 in 4 years under simple interest.
truth: The annual rate is 5%.
false: The annual rate is 20%.
reason: The 20% total increase is spread over four years under simple interest.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: ₹1000 earns 10% annual compound interest for two years, without deposits or withdrawals.
truth: The second year's interest is ₹110.
false: The second year's interest is ₹100.
reason: The second year begins with ₹1100, so 10% of that amount is ₹110.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A sum doubles every fixed number of years at a fixed compound growth rate.
truth: It takes two such periods to become four times the original sum.
false: It takes four such periods to become four times the original sum.
reason: Each period multiplies the balance by two, so two periods give 2×2 = 4.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Real numbers x and y satisfy x+y=8 and xy=12.
truth: The value of x²+y² is 40.
false: The value of x²+y² is 64.
reason: Squaring the sum includes an extra 2xy term, which must be subtracted.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A quadratic has roots 2 and 5 and leading coefficient 1.
truth: Its equation is x²−7x+10=0.
false: Its equation is x²+7x+10=0.
reason: Expand (x−2)(x−5). The sum of roots enters with a negative sign.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A shop sells pens at ₹10 and notebooks at ₹30. A purchase of 8 items costs ₹160.
truth: The purchase contains 4 notebooks.
false: The purchase contains 6 notebooks.
reason: Let n be notebooks, leaving 8−n pens. Then 30n+10(8−n)=160, so 20n=80.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A parent's age is currently three times a child's age. After 12 years, the parent's age will be twice the child's age.
truth: The child is currently 12 years old.
false: The child is currently 6 years old.
reason: Let the child's age be x. Then 3x+12=2(x+12), giving x=12.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: An arithmetic progression starts at 4 and has common difference 3.
truth: Its tenth term is 31.
false: Its tenth term is 34.
reason: The tenth term is nine steps after the first term, not ten steps.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: An arithmetic progression has 10 terms, first term 3 and last term 30.
truth: Its sum is 165.
false: Its sum is 330.
reason: The mean of the equally spaced terms is (3+30)/2 = 16.5. Multiply by ten.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Two positive integers have HCF 6 and LCM 60. One integer is 12.
truth: The other integer is 30.
false: The other integer is 24.
reason: For two positive integers, their product equals HCF times LCM. Divide 360 by 12.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: An integer leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5.
truth: Its square leaves remainder 4 when divided by 5.
false: Its square must leave remainder 2 when divided by 5.
reason: Write the integer as 5k+2. Squaring leaves the same remainder as 2².
formula: If n≡r mod m, n²≡r² mod m

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A positive integer is divisible by both 8 and 12.
truth: It must be divisible by 24.
false: It must be divisible by 96.
reason: A common multiple is divisible by the least common multiple. LCM(8,12)=24; 24 itself disproves the 96 claim.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: The expression is 18÷3×2, with ordinary left-to-right evaluation for equal-precedence operations.
truth: Its value is 12.
false: Its value is 3.
reason: Division and multiplication have equal precedence, so evaluate (18÷3)×2.
formula: Equal-precedence multiplication/division proceed left to right

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A container is 3/4 full and then loses 1/3 of the liquid currently in it.
truth: It remains 1/2 full.
false: It remains 5/12 full.
reason: The removed fraction applies to the present liquid. Retained liquid is (3/4)(2/3) of capacity.
formula: Remaining fraction = current fraction × retained fraction

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A length is reported to the nearest 0.1 cm as 12.3 cm.
truth: A true length of 12.34 cm is consistent with that report.
false: A true length of 12.39 cm is consistent with that report.
reason: Ordinary rounding to one decimal sends 12.34 to 12.3, while 12.39 rounds to 12.4.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:4.
truth: Its largest angle is 80°.
false: Its largest angle is 90°.
reason: The nine ratio parts sum to 180°, so each part is 20°. The largest angle has four parts.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Two similar triangles have corresponding side lengths in the ratio 2:5.
truth: Their areas are in the ratio 4:25.
false: Their areas are in the ratio 2:5.
reason: Area scales with the square of the linear scale factor.
formula: Area ratio = square of side ratio

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A rectangle has sides 6 cm and 8 cm.
truth: Its diagonal is 10 cm.
false: Its diagonal is 14 cm.
reason: The sides and diagonal form a right triangle. Add squared sides before taking the square root.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Points P=(−2,3) and Q=(4,−1) are endpoints of a segment.
truth: Their midpoint is (1,1).
false: Their midpoint is (2,2).
reason: Average the two x-coordinates and separately average the two y-coordinates.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A line rises by 6 units when moving 3 units to the right.
truth: Its slope is 2.
false: Its slope is 1/2.
reason: Slope is vertical change divided by horizontal change, not its reciprocal.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: An acute angle in a right triangle has opposite side 3 and hypotenuse 5.
truth: Its cosine is 4/5.
false: Its cosine is 3/5.
reason: The adjacent side is 4 by Pythagoras. Cosine is adjacent divided by hypotenuse; 3/5 is sine.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: From a point on level ground 20 m from a tower's base, the angle of elevation to its top is 45°. Ignore observer height.
truth: The tower is 20 m high.
false: The tower is 20√2 m high.
reason: Tangent 45° equals one, so vertical height equals horizontal distance. The hypotenuse is not the height.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A solid cube of side 4 cm is melted and recast into cubes of side 2 cm without loss.
truth: Eight smaller cubes are obtained.
false: Four smaller cubes are obtained.
reason: Volume is conserved. The large cube has 64 cm³ and each small cube has 8 cm³.
formula: Count = original volume / each new volume

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A cylinder's radius doubles while its height is halved.
truth: Its volume doubles.
false: Its volume stays unchanged.
reason: Radius contributes a square factor of four, while height contributes a factor of one half.
formula: V = πr²h; volume factor = radius factor² × height factor

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A square of side 10 cm has a circular hole of radius 2 cm cut from it.
truth: The remaining area is 100−4π cm².
false: The remaining area is 100−2π cm².
reason: Subtract the circle's area, πr², from the square's area. Circumference is not an area.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A factory's output increases from 200 units to 250, then returns to 200.
truth: The return change is a 20% decrease.
false: The return change is a 25% decrease.
reason: The decrease is measured against the new base 250. The 50-unit decrease is 50/250.
formula: Decrease percentage = fall / starting value of decrease ×100

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A nonzero real number x satisfies x+1/x=3.
truth: The value of x²+1/x² is 7.
false: The value of x²+1/x² is 9.
reason: Squaring includes the cross term 2x(1/x)=2; subtract it.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A sum is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2:3:5. B receives ₹90.
truth: A and C together receive ₹210.
false: A and C together receive ₹180.
reason: Three parts are ₹90, so one part is ₹30. A and C receive seven parts.
formula: Part value = known share / its ratio parts

subject: Mathematics
scenario: Six equally efficient workers complete a job in 8 days. The same work must be done in 4 days at the same rate per worker.
truth: Twelve workers are needed.
false: Three workers are needed.
reason: Total work is 48 worker-days. Halving the time requires twice as many workers.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: The average of four readings is 15. A fifth reading is added and the new average is 16.
truth: The fifth reading is 20.
false: The fifth reading is 16.
reason: The old sum is 60 and new sum is 80. Their difference is the added reading.
formula: Added value = new count × new mean − old count × old mean

subject: Mathematics
scenario: A fair six-sided die is rolled. Let A mean an even result and B mean a result greater than 4.
truth: A and B are not mutually exclusive.
false: A and B are mutually exclusive.
reason: The result 6 belongs to both events. A shared possible outcome disproves mutual exclusivity.

subject: Mathematics
scenario: An exterior angle of a triangle is 110° and one of its two remote interior angles is 45°.
truth: The other remote interior angle is 65°.
false: The other remote interior angle is 25°.
reason: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
formula: Other remote angle = exterior − known remote

subject: Mathematics
scenario: For real x, the equation (x−3)²=0 is considered.
truth: It has the single distinct solution x=3.
false: It has two distinct solutions, x=3 and x=−3.
reason: A real square is zero only when its base is zero. The repeated root does not give a second distinct value.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A rule states: whenever relay R operates, lamp L glows. Lamp L is not glowing. Assume the rule has no exceptions.
truth: Relay R has not operated.
false: Relay R must have operated.
reason: This is the contrapositive: R implies L, so not L implies not R.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A rule states: if a card is valid, a gate opens. The gate is observed to be open; there may be other opening mechanisms.
truth: The observation alone does not establish that the card is valid.
false: The open gate proves that a valid card was used.
reason: A sufficient condition is not necessarily necessary. Other mechanisms can produce the same observation.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Every copper item in a collection is a conductor. Some ornaments in the collection are copper.
truth: Some ornaments in the collection are conductors.
false: Every conductor in the collection is a copper ornament.
reason: The particular ornaments known to be copper inherit conductor status. The premises do not classify all conductors.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: No red token is square. Every token in box P is square.
truth: No token in box P is red.
false: Every non-red token must be in box P.
reason: The sets red and square are disjoint, and box P is inside square. Nothing states that all non-red tokens belong to P.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: All alpha objects are beta objects. All beta objects are gamma objects. No existence assumption is made.
truth: Every alpha object is a gamma object.
false: At least one alpha object must exist.
reason: Universal inclusion chains support another inclusion but do not, by themselves, assert that the smaller set has a member.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Some technicians are musicians. Some musicians are cyclists. These are the only premises.
truth: It is possible that no technician is a cyclist.
false: At least one technician must be a cyclist.
reason: The two mentioned subsets of musicians may be different people. Their overlap is not forced.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Exactly one of switches A and B is on. Switch A is off.
truth: Switch B is on.
false: Switch B is off.
reason: Exactly one requires one on state and excludes both-off and both-on arrangements.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: At least one of sensors X and Y is active. Sensor X is active.
truth: Sensor Y's state is not determined.
false: Sensor Y must be inactive.
reason: At least one permits one or both to be active. Knowing X is active does not determine Y.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Only employees with permits may enter a room. Ravi has entered in accordance with that rule.
truth: Ravi has a permit.
false: Every employee with a permit must have entered.
reason: Entry requires a permit, but having permission does not force entry.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A is taller than B, B is taller than C, and D is taller than A.
truth: D is taller than C.
false: C is taller than D.
reason: Chaining the comparisons gives D>A>B>C.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Four distinct scores satisfy P>Q, R>P and Q>S.
truth: R is the highest of the four.
false: P is the highest of the four.
reason: The complete ordering is R>P>Q>S.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Meena is fifth from the front and seventh from the back in a line with no ties.
truth: There are 11 people in the line.
false: There are 12 people in the line.
reason: The two counts include Meena twice, so subtract one.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: In a line of 20 people, R is eighth from the front. Four people leave, all of whom stood ahead of R.
truth: R becomes fourth from the front.
false: R becomes twelfth from the front.
reason: Only the number of people ahead matters for the front rank. It falls by four.
formula: New front rank = old rank − departures ahead

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A person walks 6 m east, 8 m north, then 6 m west.
truth: The final position is 8 m north of the starting point.
false: The final position is 20 m north of the starting point.
reason: East and west displacements cancel. Total path length is not straight-line displacement.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A person faces west, turns right, then turns right again.
truth: The person now faces east.
false: The person now faces north.
reason: A right turn from west gives north; the second right turn gives east.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A walker goes 3 m north and 4 m east. No further motion occurs.
truth: The shortest distance back to the start is 5 m.
false: The shortest distance back to the start is 7 m.
reason: The direct route is the hypotenuse of a right triangle; 7 m is the travelled path length.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: P is north of Q. R is east of P. S is directly south of R at the same north-south level as Q.
truth: S is east of Q.
false: S is west of Q.
reason: The vertical offset is cancelled by moving south to Q's level; the eastward offset remains.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Arun is the son of Bela. Bela is the sister of Charu. The terms have their ordinary family meanings.
truth: Charu is a sibling of Arun's mother.
false: Charu must be Arun's maternal uncle.
reason: The sibling relationship is certain, but Charu's gender has not been specified, so uncle is not forced.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: P is the brother of Q. Q is the mother of R. P and Q share the same parents.
truth: P is R's maternal uncle.
false: P is R's paternal grandfather.
reason: P is a male sibling of R's mother, which defines maternal uncle.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A is B's daughter. B is C's father.
truth: A and C share a father.
false: A must be older than C.
reason: The shared father follows directly. No ages or birth order are stated.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A code replaces each letter with the next alphabet letter, wrapping Z to A. The word ZAP is encoded.
truth: The code is ABQ.
false: The code is AAQ.
reason: Apply the rule to every letter: Z→A, A→B and P→Q.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A code reverses a word first and then advances every letter by one, wrapping Z to A. The input is CAT.
truth: The output is UBD.
false: The output is DBU.
reason: Reversing CAT gives TAC; advancing T,A,C gives U,B,D. Order of operations matters.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: In a puzzle, the symbol ★ is defined by a★b=2a+b. It has no other meaning.
truth: 3★4 equals 10.
false: 3★4 equals 14.
reason: Substitute a=3 and b=4 into the given definition; do not assume ordinary multiplication.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A puzzle defines a◇b=a²−b². Evaluate 5◇3.
truth: The result is 16.
false: The result is 4.
reason: The definition subtracts squares, rather than squaring the difference.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: The task is to determine a positive integer x. Statement I says x is a multiple of 3 less than 10. Statement II says x is even.
truth: The two statements together determine x=6.
false: Statement I alone determines x=6.
reason: Statement I permits 3,6,9. Adding evenness leaves only 6; neither statement alone fixes x.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: The task is to find a rectangle's area. Statement I gives length 8 cm. Statement II gives perimeter 28 cm.
truth: The two statements together are sufficient.
false: Statement II alone is sufficient.
reason: Together they give width 14−8 = 6 and area 48. Perimeter alone permits different rectangles with different areas.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: The task is to decide whether integer n is divisible by 6. Statement I says n is divisible by 2. Statement II says n is divisible by 3.
truth: The two statements together answer yes.
false: Statement I alone answers yes.
reason: Divisibility by both coprime factors 2 and 3 gives divisibility by 6. Even numbers need not be divisible by 3.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Every device in set A is also in B, and no device in B is in C.
truth: A and C have no common member.
false: Every device outside A must be in C.
reason: Any A member would also be B, which cannot be C. The premises do not classify everything outside A.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A collection has 12 round objects, 9 blue objects and 4 objects that are both round and blue.
truth: There are 17 objects that are round or blue.
false: There are 21 distinct objects that are round or blue.
reason: The four shared objects were counted twice in 12+9 and must be subtracted once.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Four people occupy seats 1 to 4 from left to right. A is in seat 1, B is immediately right of C, and D is in seat 4.
truth: C is in seat 2 and B is in seat 3.
false: B is in seat 2 and C is in seat 3.
reason: Only seats 2 and 3 remain. The stated right-neighbour relationship fixes their order.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Three tasks X, Y and Z must all be completed. Y must follow X, and Z must follow Y.
truth: X,Y,Z is the only allowed order.
false: X,Z,Y is an allowed order.
reason: The precedence chain is X before Y before Z; swapping Y and Z violates the second condition.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Three labelled boxes contain a key in exactly one box. The key is not in box A and is not in box C.
truth: The key is in box B.
false: The key may be in both B and C.
reason: The exactly-one condition and both exclusions leave only box B.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A committee must include exactly two of P,Q,R. P and Q cannot serve together.
truth: The feasible pairs are P,R and Q,R.
false: R may be excluded by choosing P,Q.
reason: The only pair without R violates the incompatibility rule, so both allowed pairs contain R.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A maintenance procedure requires isolation before inspection and inspection before restoration.
truth: Restoration cannot be first in a compliant execution.
false: Inspection may precede isolation in a compliant execution.
reason: The explicit precedence conditions give isolation, then inspection, then restoration.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: At exactly 3:30 on an ideal analogue clock, the minute hand is at 180° clockwise from 12.
truth: The smaller angle between the hands is 75°.
false: The smaller angle between the hands is 90°.
reason: The hour hand has moved to 105°, not stayed at 90°. The difference is 180−105 = 75°.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A correctly running clock's minute hand turns through 150° from its starting position.
truth: Twenty-five minutes have elapsed.
false: Thirty minutes have elapsed.
reason: The minute hand moves 360° in 60 minutes, or 6° per minute.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Today is Wednesday. A task is scheduled 17 days from today.
truth: The task falls on Saturday.
false: The task falls on Friday.
reason: Seventeen days is two complete weeks plus three days. Wednesday plus three days is Saturday.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A non-leap year begins on Monday.
truth: The next year begins on Tuesday.
false: The next year begins on Wednesday.
reason: A non-leap year contains 365 days, which is 52 weeks plus one day.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A sequence is defined, rather than guessed, by a1=2 and a(n+1)=2a(n)+1.
truth: Its fourth term is 23.
false: Its fourth term is 15.
reason: The successive terms are 2,5,11,23 under the explicit recurrence.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A sequence alternates adding 3 and multiplying by 2, starting at 4 with the addition step first.
truth: Its first four terms are 4,7,14,17.
false: Its first four terms are 4,8,11,22.
reason: Follow the given first operation and alternate: add 3, double, add 3.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Letters advance by successive steps +1,+2,+3 from A, without wrapping during these steps.
truth: The four displayed letters are A,B,D,G.
false: The four displayed letters are A,B,C,D.
reason: Positions are 1,2,4,7 after cumulative advances, corresponding to A,B,D,G.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A letter sequence starts at Y and advances three positions each time, wrapping after Z.
truth: The next two letters are B and E.
false: The next two letters are A and D.
reason: From Y, three advances are Z,A,B. Three more advances give C,D,E.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Items are classified by whether they are perfect squares. The list is 16,25,36,45.
truth: 45 is the only item outside the square class.
false: 36 is the only item outside the square class.
reason: The first three are 4²,5² and 6². No integer square lies between 36 and 49.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A rule groups integers having exactly two positive divisors. The candidates are 2,9,11,15.
truth: Exactly two candidates belong to the group.
false: Exactly three candidates belong to the group.
reason: Numbers with exactly two positive divisors are prime. Here 2 and 11 qualify; 9 and 15 are composite.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: The relation in a numeric analogy is explicitly defined as mapping n to n³. The pair 3:27 is followed by 4:?.
truth: The missing value is 64.
false: The missing value is 16.
reason: Use the stated cube relation, not a different relation suggested by one example.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: In a relation puzzle, each word is paired with its letter count, counting every letter once. TRAIN is paired with 5.
truth: SIGNAL is paired with 6.
false: SIGNAL is paired with 5.
reason: SIGNAL contains S,I,G,N,A,L, which are six letters.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: On a chart, Monday has 12 faults and Tuesday has 8. Only these two days are under consideration.
truth: Monday accounts for 60% of the two-day total.
false: Monday accounts for 150% of the two-day total.
reason: The denominator is the combined total 20. The 150% ratio compares Monday to Tuesday, which is a different question.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Two odd integers are added.
truth: Their sum must be even.
false: Their sum must be odd.
reason: Writing them as 2a+1 and 2b+1 gives 2(a+b+1), a multiple of two.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A table rule states that the third entry in each row equals the product of the first two entries minus the first. A row begins 4,7.
truth: The missing third entry is 24.
false: The missing third entry is 28.
reason: Apply the full stated rule, including subtraction of the first entry.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A square tile has a dot only at its top-left corner. It is rotated 90° clockwise in its own plane.
truth: The dot moves to the top-right corner.
false: The dot moves to the bottom-left corner.
reason: A clockwise quarter-turn takes the top-left corner to the top-right. Bottom-left would correspond to a counterclockwise quarter-turn.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: A survey states that all 40 devices inspected passed a test; no other devices were inspected.
truth: The statement establishes a result for the 40 inspected devices.
false: The statement proves that every uninspected device will pass.
reason: A result for an inspected subset does not logically establish the same result for every unobserved member.

subject: Reasoning
scenario: Exactly three lamps are on among A,B,C,D. Lamp D is off.
truth: A,B and C must all be on.
false: At least one of A,B,C must be off.
reason: With one named lamp off and exactly three on in a four-lamp set, every remaining lamp must be on.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A household's nominal income remains fixed while the overall price level rises.
truth: Its purchasing power generally falls.
false: Its purchasing power generally rises.
reason: With the same money and higher prices, the household can generally purchase fewer goods and services. This describes the purchasing-power effect of inflation.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A person can attend only one of two free training sessions. The chosen session yields a benefit valued at 500 units and the rejected best alternative at 300 units.
truth: The opportunity cost is the 300-unit benefit forgone.
false: The opportunity cost is zero because neither session charges a fee.
reason: Opportunity cost includes the best alternative benefit sacrificed, not just a cash payment.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A basket costs ₹100 one year and ₹110 the next, with quantities unchanged.
truth: The basket price has risen by 10%.
false: The basket price has risen by 110%.
reason: The increase is ₹10 compared with the original ₹100. The new level and the percentage change are different quantities.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A student spends an evening studying instead of taking an available paid shift. There is no tuition charge for the evening study.
truth: The forgone shift income can be part of the opportunity cost of studying.
false: The opportunity cost must be zero because the study itself is free.
reason: The relevant sacrifice is the best alternative forgone, including income that could have been earned.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A point moves due north from 10° south latitude, crosses the Equator, and reaches 10° north latitude.
truth: It has changed from the Southern Hemisphere to the Northern Hemisphere.
false: It has necessarily changed from the Eastern Hemisphere to the Western Hemisphere.
reason: The Equator separates north and south. Longitude, not crossing the Equator, determines east-west hemisphere classification.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: Two places lie at the same latitude but at different longitudes.
truth: Their east-west positions can differ even though their north-south angular positions match.
false: They must be the same place because their latitude matches.
reason: Latitude specifies only one coordinate. Longitude is also needed to distinguish locations along that parallel.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A diagram labels Earth's layers outward to inward as crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.
truth: The mantle is placed between the crust and the core.
false: The mantle is placed outside the crust.
reason: The crust is the outer solid layer; the mantle lies beneath it and above the core.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A student compares Earth's oceans by surface area using the standard named oceans.
truth: The Pacific exceeds the Atlantic in surface area.
false: The Arctic exceeds the Pacific in surface area.
reason: The Pacific is the largest ocean; the Arctic is much smaller. This comparison concerns surface area, not a particular coastline length.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A map marks the Tropic of Cancer near 23.5° north and the Equator at 0° latitude.
truth: Both lines are parallels of latitude.
false: Both lines are meridians of longitude.
reason: They describe north-south angular location relative to the Equator. Meridians instead run from pole to pole and identify longitude.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A circuit transfers 15 coulombs of charge in 3 seconds.
truth: Its average current is 5 amperes.
false: Its average current is 45 amperes.
reason: Current is charge passing per unit time. Multiply would give the wrong dimensions.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A 2 kg body accelerates at 3 m/s² under a net force.
truth: The net force is 6 newtons.
false: The net force is 6 joules.
reason: Mass times acceleration has units kg·m/s², named newtons. Joules measure energy.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A laboratory labels two samples Na and N using chemical element symbols.
truth: Na denotes sodium and N denotes nitrogen.
false: Both labels denote sodium.
reason: Element symbols are case-sensitive identifiers. Na and N are different symbols for different elements.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A sample of ordinary dry air is compared by volume of its principal gases.
truth: Nitrogen is more abundant than oxygen.
false: Oxygen makes up roughly 78% of the dry air.
reason: Nitrogen accounts for roughly 78% and oxygen for roughly 21% of ordinary dry air by volume.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A diagram follows blood from the heart through vessels and back to the heart.
truth: The heart supplies the pumping action for circulation.
false: The stomach supplies the main pumping action for circulation.
reason: The muscular heart drives blood circulation. Digestion in the stomach has a different principal role.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: Pure water is considered at 25°C under ordinary conditions.
truth: Neutrality corresponds approximately to pH 7.
false: Neutrality at these conditions requires pH 1.
reason: At 25°C, pure water has equal hydrogen- and hydroxide-ion concentrations and approximately pH 7. A pH near 1 is strongly acidic.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A solution at 25°C has pH 3, and another at the same temperature has pH 5.
truth: The first has approximately 100 times the hydrogen-ion activity of the second.
false: The first has approximately two times the hydrogen-ion activity of the second.
reason: The pH scale is logarithmic. A difference of two pH units corresponds to a factor of 10².

subject: General Awareness
scenario: An astronomy description identifies a planet by its especially prominent ring system made largely of ice particles.
truth: Saturn matches that description.
false: Mercury matches that description.
reason: Saturn is noted for its extensive, easily recognized ring system. Mercury does not have such a ring system.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A study note distinguishes the date of adoption of India's Constitution from its principal commencement date.
truth: 26 November 1949 is the adoption date and 26 January 1950 the principal commencement date.
false: 26 January 1950 is the adoption date and 26 November 1949 the principal commencement date.
reason: Adoption and commencement are different milestones; the latter is commemorated as Republic Day.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A student organizes constitutional notes into Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy.
truth: Part III is the appropriate main heading for Fundamental Rights and Part IV for Directive Principles.
false: Part IV is the appropriate main heading for Fundamental Rights and Part III for Directive Principles.
reason: The two sets of provisions occupy different parts of the Constitution; interchanging their labels misclassifies them.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: An English-language civics chart uses the alternative names of India's two houses of Parliament.
truth: Council of States refers to Rajya Sabha, while House of the People refers to Lok Sabha.
false: Council of States refers to Lok Sabha, while House of the People refers to Rajya Sabha.
reason: These are the respective constitutional names of the two houses; they are not interchangeable.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A history note links the 1930 Dandi March with opposition to the British salt monopoly.
truth: Salt, rather than an income-tax filing rule, was central to that protest.
false: The note should replace salt with railway ticket tax as the central issue.
reason: The march and breaking of the salt law challenged colonial control over salt and the associated tax.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A cultural-history exhibit pairs Jana Gana Mana with its composer.
truth: Rabindranath Tagore is the appropriate composer for that pairing.
false: Alexander Fleming is the appropriate composer for that pairing.
reason: Tagore composed Jana Gana Mana. Fleming belongs to the history of penicillin, not the composition of the anthem.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A science-history timeline places Fleming's observation of the antibacterial effect of Penicillium mould in 1928.
truth: It links that observation with the discovery of penicillin.
false: It links that observation with the discovery of the planet Saturn.
reason: The observation was a key milestone in penicillin's discovery. Later development into a widely usable drug involved further work.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A label gives a force as 12 N and an electric current as 2 A.
truth: The symbols correspond to newtons and amperes respectively.
false: The symbols correspond to newtons and coulombs respectively.
reason: A is the symbol for ampere, the SI unit of electric current; coulomb is the unit of charge and uses C.

subject: General Awareness
scenario: A vessel crosses the Equator while staying in the Pacific Ocean.
truth: Crossing the Equator does not require crossing an ocean boundary.
false: Every Equator crossing necessarily leaves the Pacific for the Atlantic.
reason: The Equator is a latitude line crossing the Pacific itself, not a boundary between those two oceans.
